etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French spirale, from Medieval Latin spiralis, from Latin spīra, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra, “wreath, coil, twist”).

definitions.definition: (geometry) A curve that is the locus of a point that rotates about a fixed point while continuously increasing its distance from that point.
A self-sustaining process with a lot of momentum involved, so it is difficult to accelerate or stop it at once.

quote.citation: 2015, Jane Ward, Not Gay, New York University Press, →ISBN, page xi:
quote.text: My beloved friends and family who sustained and grounded me as I fell into the rabbit hole of this project or down the spiral of new parenthood.

definitions.definition: (rail transport) A section of track that forms a circle and crosses over itself, used for gaining height in mountainous territory.

quote.citation: 1877, H. F. Blandford, Indian Meteorologist's Vade-mecum, page 140:
quote.text: The formation of tornados and water-spouts is very probably identical with that of dust-storms and "devils," viz., a sudden disturbance of the vertical equilibrium of the atmosphere, where by an upward rush of air is generated, which rapidly becomes spiral.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move along the path of a spiral or helix.
